chapter: Stuff Smith Trio and New York
title: Eubie Blake's conducting lesson, Jones's 1945 marriage and Cafe Society
summary: Eubie gave Jones his first conducting lesson; Jones dates his marriage to 1945 and recalls Cafe Society with J. C. Heard.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: You should have seen him conduct. He gave me my first conducting lesson.
How old were you?
Oh, by that time I was -- oh, let's see, I was -- I was married and everything by then.
How old were you when you got married?
Let me see. Baby, I'll get this together in a minute.
I'll bet Speedy would have remembered.
Oh, yeah. We got married in '45. That's right, because Eubie and Marion got married in '46, a year later. We both -- all of us were living in Brooklyn then, you know?
Uh-huh.
And Eubie was going to -- 1945, I should have been -- well, you can figure it out. Look in Leonard's book.
Let's see, you were born in 1918.
Yeah.
All right.
The end of 1918.
The tail end. The last couple of days.
Yeah.
Okay.
Because I'm trying to -- I'm trying to bring 1919 in, but it ain't going to work.
(Laughter)
Yeah, you see, you can get it from there. And I think I met Eubie the next year, '46. I was working at Cafe Society with J. C. Heard (PHONETIC), and that's when I first met Sarah. And --
You were working with J. C. Heard and whom?

Let's see, I'll tell you who was in the band. Budd Johnson. Well, J. C. McKibbon Al McGiven (PHONETIC). Dickie Wells and George Joyce Treadwell. It was a nice little group, you know? And Eubie was -- he took -- I think he went to NYU before I did, and studied with Rudolph Schramm, the great Schillinger teacher, you know?
Uh-huh.

And let's see, I've got to write Schramm, because I don't think he knows Speedy's Sweetie's gone. We used to hang out together, you know? There was a funny thing, you know, when I used to buy these textbooks, and I would conduct very stiff, and Eubie had a nine foot grand at his house. So we just took the "Star Spangled Banner," you see. Okay, give me
the "Star Spangled Banner," and I was conducting -- just like that. Square, you know. Right angles.
With a clenched fist?
No, no, no, no, no.
Okay.
And Eubie played it like that. I said, "Eubie, what's wrong?" He said, "That's the way you conducted me." Then he got up and his hands were very fluid and -- you know?
Uh-huh.

Very easy. Because he'd had all that experience in the pit, you know, conducting shows on Broadway, uptown, so it was -- as of now they have him as a ragtime piano player, but he's a well rounded musician, well rounded. But he just happens to be a very funny man, a great sense of humor.
He certainly does, from what I've seen of him in television interviews, and then that day we spent an hour at his house.
Oh, he's going to be funny. And he's not trying to be. He's just born that way.
Well, he's got a sense of humor, though. I mean he knows he's being funny. It's not an unconscious thing.
No, he knows he's -- well, he loves an
audience, you know.
Obviously.

All of us hams love an audience, you know? I'd like -- when I get on stage or playing or something, you -- I like it. Especially when the audience likes it. I feel like a million dollars when the audience likes it, you know, because if I fell in love with what I played I'd be nuts. But --
